nodes.title: PC hardware: Key Ideas
nodes.content: CompTIA A+ and similar exams test physical hardware: connectors, motherboard layout, power, storage, RAM types. The trick is matching the symptom to the component — boot failures usually mean RAM/power/CMOS battery, slow disk means thermals or imminent failure.

flashcards.front: DDR3 vs DDR4 vs DDR5 — what changes?
flashcards.back: Each generation roughly doubles peak bandwidth and lowers operating voltage. DDR3 = 1.5V, DDR4 = 1.2V, DDR5 = 1.1V. Slots are keyed differently — you cannot physically install the wrong generation. Mixing speeds in dual-channel makes them run at the slowest speed.

flashcards.front: M.2 NVMe vs M.2 SATA vs 2.5" SATA — which is fastest?
flashcards.back: M.2 NVMe (uses PCIe lanes): 3,500-7,000 MB/s read. M.2 SATA (M.2 form factor but SATA bus): ~550 MB/s. 2.5" SATA: also ~550 MB/s. The same M.2 slot may accept both; the motherboard manual tells you which keys (B-key SATA, M-key NVMe) it supports.

flashcards.front: What does the CMOS battery do?
flashcards.back: Powers the CMOS chip that stores BIOS/UEFI settings and the real-time clock when the system is unplugged. Symptoms of a dead one: clock resets to default on every boot, BIOS settings revert, occasional 'CMOS checksum error'. Coin cell CR2032, $1 fix.

flashcards.front: POST beep codes — what do they mean?
flashcards.back: Power-On Self-Test diagnostic beeps from the motherboard speaker before video init. Single short beep = pass. Repeating short beeps = memory error. Long-short-short = video problem. Each BIOS vendor has a slightly different code chart — check the motherboard manual.

nodes.title: Windows OS fundamentals (CompTIA A+): Key Ideas
nodes.content: CompTIA A+ Core 2 tests practical Windows knowledge: edition differences, filesystem capabilities, partition table formats, and the 32-bit vs 64-bit memory ceiling. Understanding these distinctions helps diagnose installation issues, hardware compatibility, and storage configuration questions on the exam.

flashcards.front: 32-bit Windows vs 64-bit — what is the memory address limit of each?
flashcards.back: 32-bit Windows can address a maximum of 4 GB of RAM (2^32 bytes). In practice, user applications get ~2 GB and the kernel gets ~2 GB; hardware-reserved addresses reduce usable RAM further (often ~3.2 GB visible). 64-bit Windows supports up to 128 GB (Home) or 2 TB (Pro/Enterprise) depending on edition. For any modern workstation with > 4 GB RAM, a 64-bit OS is mandatory.

flashcards.front: NTFS vs FAT32 vs exFAT — compare for exam purposes.
flashcards.back: FAT32: max file size 4 GB, max volume 8 TB, no permissions or journaling — legacy, used for USB drives that must work on old systems. NTFS: max file size 256 TB, full ACL permissions, journaling, encryption (EFS), compression — required for Windows system drives. exFAT: no 4 GB file limit, no permissions/journaling — designed for flash drives and SD cards that must work across Windows and macOS without NTFS overhead. Use exFAT for large external media, NTFS for internal drives.

flashcards.front: MBR vs GPT partition tables — key differences?
flashcards.back: MBR (Master Boot Record): max disk size 2 TB, max 4 primary partitions (or 3 primary + 1 extended with logical drives), 32-bit sector addressing. Legacy BIOS only. GPT (GUID Partition Table): supports disks > 2 TB, up to 128 partitions, 64-bit addressing, backup partition table at the end of disk, required for UEFI boot. All modern systems should use GPT; MBR is only needed for Windows XP compatibility or very old hardware.

flashcards.front: Windows editions — what separates Home, Pro, and Enterprise?
flashcards.back: Home: consumer features, no domain join, no Group Policy, no Remote Desktop host, no BitLocker (encrypted removable drives only). Pro: adds domain join, Group Policy, Remote Desktop, BitLocker, Hyper-V, up to 2 CPUs. Enterprise: adds AppLocker, DirectAccess, BranchCache, advanced Credential Guard, longer LTSC support channel — requires volume licensing. The A+ exam often tests whether a specific feature requires Pro or Enterprise.

nodes.title: Order the CompTIA troubleshooting steps

data.scenario: A user's PC won't boot. Put CompTIA's troubleshooting methodology in order.

nodes.explanation: CompTIA's six-step method: identify the problem, establish a theory of probable cause, test the theory, establish a plan and implement the fix, verify full system functionality (with preventive measures), and document findings.

nodes.title: Troubleshooting methodology: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A structured troubleshooting process beats random guessing every time. The classic flow: identify the problem precisely, form a theory, test it, fix, verify, document. Most exams test that you know the flow AND can spot the layer at which the symptom originates.

flashcards.front: What's the standard troubleshooting model?
flashcards.back: CompTIA's 6-step: (1) Identify the problem (gather symptoms, questions to user, recent changes). (2) Establish a theory of probable cause. (3) Test the theory. (4) Plan and implement the fix. (5) Verify full system functionality, apply preventive measures. (6) Document everything.

flashcards.front: Top-down vs bottom-up troubleshooting on a network problem.
flashcards.back: Top-down: start at the application layer and work down — does the browser work? DNS? TCP? Routing? Bottom-up: start at the physical layer — is the cable plugged in? Link light? IP? When you suspect physical/cable, bottom-up is faster. When the user has 'a website is broken', top-down is faster.

flashcards.front: Why ask 'what changed recently'?
flashcards.back: Almost every production incident traces back to a recent change — a deploy, a config push, a vendor patch, a cert rotation. 'It was working yesterday' tells you to check today's change-log before forming an exotic theory. Recent changes are the highest-priors of the bug space.

flashcards.front: What's the divide-and-conquer technique?
flashcards.back: Bisect the path between symptom and cause. If 10 hops between client and server, test hop 5. Good → problem is past hop 5. Bad → problem is before. Two more bisections narrow it to one hop. Faster than checking every link sequentially when the chain is long.

questions.q: A Windows PC POSTs successfully but during boot displays 'Operating system not found' or 'No bootable device'. The OS install is intact (verified from a recovery USB). What's the FIRST troubleshooting step / cause to investigate?
choices: Faulty RAM stick
Wrong boot order in BIOS / UEFI OR corrupted bootloader / boot sector on
GPU failed — would show display issues, not OS-not-found
Network adapter — irrelevant to local-disk boot
questions.explanation: The BIOS/UEFI cannot locate a bootable OS. Check boot order in firmware, confirm the SSD/HDD is detected, and run startup repair or 'bootrec /fixmbr' from Windows installation media.

questions.q: A laptop user reports Wi-Fi has stopped working. Device Manager shows the wireless adapter as 'disabled'. Before any driver changes or hardware swap, what's the FIRST cheap step a technician should check?
choices: Flash the laptop's BIOS firmware to the latest version — disruptive, rarely the cause of a Wi-Fi hardware disable; check simpler causes first
Reinstall Windows — extreme resolution before checking hardware enable states; the laptop Wi-Fi adapter is shown as disabled in Device Manager, not missing
Check the laptop's Wi-Fi hardware kill switch (Fn + Wi-Fi key) or the wireless hardware switch in BIOS settings before replacing hardware
Replace the M.2 wireless card inside the laptop chassis — premature before verifying the hardware switch and Device Manager enable state
questions.explanation: Many laptops have a physical Wi-Fi switch or an Fn key combo (e.g., Fn+F2) that disables wireless. Toggle it first. If still disabled, confirm Wi-Fi is enabled in firmware before assuming a driver or hardware fault.

questions.q: A Windows user reports persistent 100% disk usage in Task Manager and a sluggish system. Foreground apps freeze briefly. SMART data shows the drive is healthy BUT under heavy I/O. What are the two most common causes a technician should rule out FIRST?
choices: Background indexing (Windows Search), AV scan, OR
Monitor causing GPU contention
Defective RAM — would manifest as BSODs or app crashes, not sustained 100% disk usage visible in Windows Task Manager
Outdated video driver — wouldn't drive 100% disk; a stale GPU driver affects rendering, not Windows storage stack I/O
questions.explanation: 100% disk usage often comes from Windows Search, antivirus scans, Windows Update servicing, or a dying mechanical drive. Inspect processes in Task Manager and run CHKDSK plus SMART checks on the drive.

questions.q: A technician powers on a workstation and hears THREE distinct beeps from the motherboard speaker; the screen stays black; no POST text. Per AMI / Award BIOS beep code tables, three beeps indicate a specific subsystem failure. What's the diagnosis?
choices: RAM problem
CMOS coin-cell drained
Failing disk — disk failures don't produce POST beeps; OS error after POST
CPU thermal protection
questions.explanation: Beep codes vary by BIOS vendor, but three beeps on AMI/Award commonly indicate a RAM issue. Reseat the DIMMs, test one stick at a time, and try alternate slots to isolate the bad module or socket.

questions.q: A user's tower powers on (fans spin, drive activity LED blinks) but the monitor stays BLACK at boot. There's no display whatsoever. What troubleshooting steps should the technician check FIRST (before any disassembly)?
choices: Push WSUS driver updates remotely to check for GPU driver issues — remote management requires a working display connection; a black screen that stays dark during boot cannot be fixed by sending remote activity
Swap the CPU to check for a failed core affecting the video output path — premature; the first step should always be checking the monitor input source before disassembling the system
Reinstall Windows to check if a corrupted OS boot process is causing the monitor to stay black — the screen stays dark before Windows loads, so reinstall activity cannot reach the problem
Check the monitor's input source (HDMI / DP selection) and reseat the GPU in its PCIe slot — these are the first hardware checks when a monitor stays black despite power-on activity
questions.explanation: Start with the simplest causes: verify the monitor is powered and set to the right input, reseat the GPU and re-check the display cable, then listen for POST beep codes that point to RAM or GPU faults.

questions.q: A Windows 10 PC won't boot — Windows reports 'Bootmgr is missing' OR 'No bootable device found'. The system disk is intact (verified). The MBR is corrupted. Which BUILT-IN command, run from Windows Recovery Environment, repairs the Master Boot Record?
choices: `sfc /scannow` — checks SYSTEM FILES integrity, not the MBR
`chkdsk /f` — repairs filesystem, not the MBR
`diskpart clean` — DESTRUCTIVE; wipes the disk, doesn't repair MBR
`bootrec /fixmbr`
questions.explanation: From the Windows Recovery Environment: 'bootrec /fixmbr' rewrites the MBR, 'bootrec /fixboot' repairs the boot sector, and 'bootrec /rebuildbcd' rebuilds the Boot Configuration Data store.

questions.q: An old mechanical HDD has slow boot times, occasional hang/freeze, audible CLICKING sound, and `Get-PhysicalDisk` shows degraded SMART attributes (reallocated sectors, pending sectors). The user reports these issues are getting more frequent. What's the diagnosis?
choices: AV misclassifying I/O — wouldn't produce clicking sounds
RAM module — would cause BSOD / app crashes, not drive clicks
HDD is failing
CPU thermal throttling — wouldn't affect drive sound or SMART
questions.explanation: Clicking, grinding, slow seeks, and freezes on an HDD point to mechanical decline. Check SMART (CrystalDiskInfo) — any 'Caution' or 'Bad' attribute means back up immediately and replace the drive.

questions.q: A user calls: 'my PC won't turn on'. No fans spin, no LEDs, completely dark. Before ANY internal hardware step, the technician should walk through the cheapest external checks. Which?
choices: Check the power cable seating at both ends, the wall outlet (test
Reinstall OS — irrelevant if the system isn't powering on
Swap motherboard — premature without ruling out power source
Replace PSU — premature without confirming AC supply first
questions.explanation: Always rule out the simple causes first: cable seated, wall outlet live, power strip on, UPS or surge protector functional, and the front-panel power LED responding when the button is pressed.

nodes.title: Windows diagnostic tools (CompTIA A+): Key Ideas
nodes.content: A+ Core 2 is heavily scenario-based: given a symptom, which tool do you open? The exam tests chkdsk for disk errors, sfc for corrupt system files, ipconfig for network config, msconfig/Task Manager for startup and performance, and Event Viewer for log analysis — knowing the exact flag or tab for each scenario is the difference between a right and wrong answer.

flashcards.front: chkdsk — what does it check and when must you schedule it?
flashcards.back: `chkdsk C:` checks for file system errors and bad sectors on a volume. With `/f` it fixes errors; with `/r` it locates bad sectors and recovers readable data (implies /f). If the target volume is the system drive (C:), Windows cannot lock it while running; you'll be prompted to schedule it for the next restart. Always run `chkdsk /r` when a user reports random file corruption or 'not formatted' errors.

flashcards.front: sfc /scannow — what does it do that chkdsk doesn't?
flashcards.back: System File Checker (`sfc /scannow`) scans all protected Windows system files and replaces corrupted or missing ones from the Windows component store (WinSxS). chkdsk checks the file system structure (allocation tables, bad sectors); sfc checks file integrity of the OS itself. Run sfc when Windows behavior is abnormal after a failed update or malware infection. Run as Administrator; requires a reboot for most replacements.

flashcards.front: ipconfig — which flags do you use for which task?
flashcards.back: `ipconfig` — show current IP/mask/gateway for all adapters. `ipconfig /all` — adds MAC address, DHCP server, DNS servers, lease times. `ipconfig /release` + `ipconfig /renew` — release and re-request a DHCP lease (fix 169.254.x.x APIPA addresses). `ipconfig /flushdns` — clear the local DNS resolver cache (fix stale DNS records). The A+ exam tests the flags, not just the command.

flashcards.front: msconfig vs Task Manager — which to use for startup items?
flashcards.back: msconfig (System Configuration) manages boot options (Safe Boot, Selective Startup) and shows services/startup items, but in Windows 8+, startup app management was moved out of msconfig into Task Manager → Startup tab. Task Manager → Startup tab shows every app set to launch at login, its publisher, and the measured startup impact (Low/Medium/High). Disable startup apps in Task Manager; use msconfig for boot flags and service troubleshooting.

questions.q: An NTFS volume on a Windows PC shows file-system errors and the user reports occasional read failures. Which built-in Windows utility SCANS the volume's metadata structure for errors, marks bad sectors, and OPTIONALLY repairs corruption?
choices: Task Manager — process / resource viewer, not a fs scanner
Device Manager — hardware enumeration, not filesystem scan
CHKDSK
Disk Defragmenter — optimises file placement, not error-scan
questions.explanation: CHKDSK (Check Disk) verifies the file system and can flag bad sectors. 'chkdsk /f' fixes logical errors; 'chkdsk /r' implies /f and additionally locates bad sectors and recovers readable data.

questions.q: An admin wants the FULL Windows network configuration: every adapter's IPv4 + IPv6, MAC, DNS servers, gateway, DHCP server, lease times, and connection-specific DNS suffix. Which built-in command outputs this in one go?
choices: `tracert hostname` — measures hops to a remote address, not local config
`ipconfig /all`
`ping 8.8.8.8` — reachability test, not config
`netstat -ano` — connection / listening sockets, not adapter config
questions.explanation: 'ipconfig' lists IP, subnet, and default gateway per adapter. 'ipconfig /all' also prints DHCP server, DNS servers, MAC address, and lease times — useful for DHCP and DNS troubleshooting.

questions.q: A Windows PC takes 3 minutes to login because too many apps auto-start. A technician wants to SEE every app configured to launch at sign-in and DISABLE the non-essential ones. Which BUILT-IN tool is the canonical place to manage startup items in Windows 10/11?
choices: Registry Editor — possible but unguarded; not the user-facing tool
Task Manager → Startup tab (or `msconfig`)
Device Manager — drivers, not startup apps
Control Panel → Programs and Features — installed-program list, not autostart
questions.explanation: Windows 10/11 exposes startup management in Task Manager's Startup tab. The legacy msconfig (System Configuration) tool also lists startup items and is handy when troubleshooting boot or sign-in delays.

questions.q: A new 4 TB SSD is plugged into a Windows PC. The disk shows up in Disk Management as 'Not Initialised'. The admin must initialise (GPT vs MBR), create a partition (volume), assign a drive letter, and format it. Which built-in Windows tool covers all these tasks?
choices: Device Manager — handles driver enumeration and device management, not partition or volume management
Task Manager — shows process and resource management, not disk partition creation or volume management
Disk Management (`diskmgmt.msc`) or `diskpart` CLI
CHKDSK — performs filesystem-error checking on an existing volume; it cannot perform partition management or volume creation
questions.explanation: Disk Management (diskmgmt.msc) creates, deletes, formats, and resizes partitions and assigns drive letters via a GUI. The diskpart CLI is the scriptable equivalent with more advanced options (used in recovery).

questions.q: Windows ships a console (devmgmt.msc) that enumerates every detected hardware device, shows which driver is installed, allows driver update / rollback / disable / uninstall, and surfaces 'Other devices' for hardware missing a driver. Which tool?
choices: Device Manager
Manages users and groups
Controls Windows Update
Manages startup apps
questions.explanation: Device Manager (devmgmt.msc) lists hardware and driver state. A yellow exclamation = driver problem; a red X = disabled. Right-click to update, roll back, or uninstall. 'View → Show hidden devices' helps in tricky cases.

questions.q: A Windows admin investigates yesterday's BSOD. They need a chronologically ordered, severity-classified record of every system event (boot, driver load, service stop, app crash, security audit, login success/fail). Which built-in tool surfaces these?
choices: Startup item manager (Task Manager → Startup)
Device Manager — drivers, not events
Event Viewer (`eventvwr.msc`)
LAN traffic monitor — Wireshark / netmon, not Event Viewer
questions.explanation: Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc) shows logs: System (hardware/driver), Application (program errors), and Security (logon/audit). Event IDs guide diagnosis — e.g., 4624 successful logon, 1000 application crash.

questions.q: A Windows admin runs into corrupted system DLLs that cause apps to crash. Microsoft ships a CLI tool that scans Windows-protected system files against a manifest hash, replacing any that don't match. Which command?
choices: `defrag c: /u` — defrag, not system-file repair
`chkdsk c: /f` — filesystem repair, not Windows-protected files
`diskpart list` — partition CLI, not system-file repair
`sfc /scannow`
questions.explanation: 'sfc /scannow' (System File Checker) scans and repairs corrupted or missing protected system files. Run from an elevated prompt. If SFC cannot repair, run 'DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth' first.

questions.q: An admin needs Windows to automatically run a PowerShell maintenance script every Tuesday at 02:00 AND on Windows event 4624 (logon). The runs must be logged and survive reboots. Which built-in Windows component?
choices: CPU scheduler thread priority — kernel scheduler, different surface
Print queue manager
Task Scheduler (`taskschd.msc`)
Logon-time auditing
questions.explanation: Task Scheduler (taskschd.msc) runs commands or scripts based on triggers (time, logon, idle, event). Windows itself uses it for updates and maintenance; admins use it for backups, cleanups, and other automation.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.front: What is the CIA triad?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.

flashcards.front: What does 'least privilege' mean?
flashcards.back: Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.

flashcards.front: What is defense in depth?
flashcards.back: Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

nodes.title: Networking fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Networking moves packets between machines using layered protocols (the OSI / TCP-IP stack). Most exam questions test routing decisions, subnetting math, the difference between L2 and L3, and how DNS / DHCP make the whole thing usable for humans.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3?
flashcards.back: L2 (data link) uses MAC addresses to deliver frames inside a single broadcast domain (a switch). L3 (network) uses IP addresses to route packets between networks (a router). Switches do L2; routers do L3.

flashcards.front: How does a subnet mask work?
flashcards.back: The mask splits an IP into a network portion (the high bits, set to 1) and a host portion (the low bits, set to 0). `/24` means the first 24 bits are network = up to 256 hosts (254 usable). `/30` is 4 IPs = 2 hosts — typical for a point-to-point link.

flashcards.front: What does DNS do?
flashcards.back: Domain Name System translates human-readable names (`example.com`) into IP addresses. A recursive resolver asks the root, the TLD server (`.com`), and finally the authoritative server for the domain. TTL controls how long answers are cached.

flashcards.front: TCP vs UDP — when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: TCP is reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — use it when every byte matters (HTTP, SSH, SMTP). UDP is lightweight, no handshake, no retransmit — use it for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, anywhere latency beats reliability.

questions.q: A Windows host fails to obtain a DHCP lease. Instead of an error, Windows auto-assigns itself an address in a specific reserved /16 range. The host can talk to other APIPA-addressed hosts on the same LAN but NOT to anything via the gateway. Which range?
choices: Automatic PUBLIC IP
Automated Prefix IP Assignment
Advanced Private IP Auto-configuration
APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing)
questions.explanation: APIPA assigns a 169.254.x.x address when Windows cannot reach a DHCP server. Seeing 169.254.x.x means DHCP failed — check the cable, the DHCP scope, and reachability to the DHCP server.

questions.q: Before consulting DNS, Windows reads `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` to map a hostname directly to an IP. Used for local overrides / blocking malicious domains / testing. The file requires admin rights to edit. Which is this?
choices: Startup-app manager
The hosts file
Defender Firewall rule store
Driver-tracking database
questions.explanation: The hosts file (C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts) overrides DNS for local name resolution. Format: '192.168.1.10 server1.local'. Malware sometimes edits it to redirect banking sites — review during incidents.

questions.q: A user types `https://news.example.com` in a browser. Before the HTTPS request can leave, the OS asks a SERVICE running on port 53 to translate the hostname to a routable IP via a hierarchical authoritative system (root → .com → example.com → news). Which service?
choices: TLS handshake — performs encryption negotiation after hostname resolution; it does not perform hierarchical name lookup
DNS — hierarchical hostname-to-IP resolution over UDP/TCP 53
DHCP — leases IP addresses to LAN clients automatically; it does not perform hierarchical hostname resolution
Internet routing via BGP — routes packets between autonomous systems based on IP prefixes; it does not resolve hostnames or operate hierarchically by hostname label
questions.explanation: DNS turns names like www.example.com into IP addresses. Resolution order: browser cache → OS cache → hosts file → local resolver → ISP/public DNS → authoritative DNS. Troubleshoot with nslookup or dig.

questions.q: An admin needs to override DNS for a single hostname WITHOUT changing DNS servers — e.g., point `internal-test.example.com` to `10.0.5.42` only on this PC. Which Windows file lets them do this?
choices: `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts`
Windows Trusted-certificates store
Windows SAM database
Windows DHCP scope configuration
questions.explanation: C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts maps hostnames to IPs locally and takes precedence over DNS. Used for dev (dev.local → 127.0.0.1) and ad-blocking; abused by malware to redirect domains.

questions.q: A Windows host is on a corporate LAN. The admin moves the cable to a different VLAN. Stale DHCP info is still cached. To force a clean re-acquire: first DROP the current lease, then REQUEST a new one. Which two commands?
choices: Resets Defender Firewall to clear the current network profile
`ipconfig /release` (drops the current DHCP
Clear the current DNS cache with `ipconfig /flushdns`
Reload the current NIC driver via Device Manager
questions.explanation: 'ipconfig /release' drops the DHCP lease; 'ipconfig /renew' requests a fresh address. Use both when a device has the wrong IP, a duplicate IP, or APIPA (169.254.x.x). 'ipconfig /flushdns' clears stale DNS entries.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

distractors.fullName: A scheduled midnight self-diagnostic that tests power delivery and logs errors post-shutdown
A user-launched self-test that measures power consumption of the CPU at startup
An OEM firmware push that self-installs microcode patches before handing power to the OS
